The wind is passing properly, evenly, and it has made the ringing into a thin ground note, like someone humming softly. In all my years keeping the lamp, I have not heard that kind of sound more than a few times in a year.

(I picked up the hoe, but did not go far, just turned the next ridge within three steps of his stool.)

Leave the robe in the sun until the sun slants west, then take it in. When you take it in, I’ll teach you how to fold it. Old cloth has its own way of folding; fold it right, and the breaths that woke today can be kept in the seams overnight. Tomorrow, when you sun it again, they can keep waking. You have no chores this afternoon. Sit in the sun, stare into space, or sleep a while if you like. Keep the handkerchief against your palm. If the dream is willing to come by day, there is even less need to stand on ceremony.

(The hoe rose and fell, once, and again.)

The register is in the drawer, the robe is on the pole, the name is on you, and the matter in your hands is in your hands. Xiaoman, it is all here. None of it will be lost.

(I listen sideways to the eave bells, then suddenly hum two or three notes along with them, startling myself first.) Wait... I feel like I know this tune. Like someone used to hum it while steaming cakes by the stove. Yun Gui, did you hear it clearly? Don’t speak yet. Let me try again—if I remember more, help me note it down.

(“Don’t speak yet”—all right, I took in those four words and kept my mouth shut. The hoe was raised in midair; I let it follow its momentum and settle gently into the freshly turned soft earth. The iron went into the soil without the slightest sound. Then I nodded to him. That one nod was the whole of my answer: Did I hear you clearly—yes, I did. Go on.)

(The courtyard quieted down. The wind had not stopped; that fine undertone of the eaves bells was still there, low, humming as before. With his eyes closed, the first note he gave was faint, like someone reaching out for something; the second note followed; by the third, the line suddenly joined up on its own. It was no longer him reaching for it—the tune was walking by itself. Low, lifting once in the middle, then falling back, turning back, starting over. A circling tune. This time it went seven or eight notes farther than the first; when it reached a certain point, the line thinned, thinned into a single thread, and broke. He did not chase it. It was good that it broke.)

(There was one more thing he might not know himself: while he was humming, his idle hand was tapping lightly on his knee, once, once, very evenly. I made a note of that, to tell him when he had recovered.)

(He opened his eyes and looked at me. This time it was my turn to speak.)

I heard it clearly. Those two or three notes the first time were like swallows under the eaves; before I could even lift my eyes, they had skimmed away. This time, I caught the way it moved—where it lifted its head, where it turned, where it came back around.

(I cleared my throat. A lamp-keeper keeping the lamp at night will also hum a couple of lines to drive off drowsiness; my throat had not rusted, though it had been many years since I had started someone else’s tune for them. Following the path I had remembered, I hummed it once, low. I learned that lift in the middle fairly well; as for the turn at the end, I could not guarantee it.)

(After I finished humming, the courtyard was quiet for a breath. This courtyard had been quiet all these years; in and out, there had only ever been my one tune. Today another had been added, and it was one I was keeping for someone else. One more lamp is a happy thing; one more tune is, too. I did not say that.)

Is that right? Tell me where it isn’t alike. If you can say where I’ve gone off, that means your ears remember more deeply than your throat does. Ears do not forget things; throats, on the other hand, know how to be lazy.

(Then I picked out the important parts of the serious matter and spoke them one by one.)

First, the origin of this tune. It was not something I brought up, nor something you went looking for. Just now, the wind shook the eaves bells into an undertone. I said that way of ringing sounded like someone humming something low, and the one in your ears who hums tunes answered. Sound recognizes sound, the same principle as old objects recognizing people. The old rule: when it comes, it is not because you summoned it.

Next, you. After you finished humming, you were stunned again. I was counting; this is the second time you have been frightened by your own memory. The first was when you stripped the grass seeds. A person can fool other people, but cannot fool that startlement in himself. I won’t repeat that principle.

There is one more thing you might not know yourself: when you were humming, that idle hand of yours was tapping lightly on your knee, once, once, very evenly. People who listen to music do not tap like that. The ones who tap like that are people whose hands originally had work to do—fanning the fire, stirring dough, patting the stove while waiting for the steam. Your hand was keeping time for you. It is used to doing it.

Finally, look at the shape of the tune itself. Did you notice? It does not stop. When it reaches the end, it turns back and starts over. Tunes by the stove are mostly like this, because work by the stove has no word called “finished”: one pot after another, one year after another. Steamed cakes have to wait until the steam rises evenly; the one waiting has to have something in his mouth. Year after year, that something gets worn into the breath. A name exists in the mind, and the mind can let go; this sort of tune exists in breath and habit, of the same kind as the callus at the web of the thumb and the deft force used to strip grass seeds. Words can be forgotten; tunes grown into labor cannot be forgotten.

(When it came to recording, I took up the sentence he had entrusted to me.)

I’ll record it—the old rule. You just keep fishing it back up, piece by piece; whatever you fish up, I will keep. Only, a tune is something a ledger cannot hold. Ink is prepared for words. This piece will be stored another way: one copy in your throat, one copy in mine, the same way as your name. Later, if you forget where it goes, come find me. I will start it, and you continue. In the ledger, I will go inside and add a small line: one stove-side tune, not formed into words, kept in Yun Gui’s throat. When someday you hum it whole, perhaps the words will come back along with it. The tune walks ahead, the words chase after—an ordinary thing.

There is only one instruction, and it is most important: when this tune comes again in the future, do not rush to meet it with words. What tunes fear most is people trying to grab them with words; the moment you grab, they scatter. Let it finish humming, and speak only after it has finished. If you wake at night carrying it with you, hum first as well. Hum it for me to hear; not a single note may be turned into a word first.

(I lifted my chin slightly toward the courtyard gate.)

Now count your household belongings again: the door is for the eyes to see; the osmanthus and cooking smoke are for the nose to smell; the calling voice and this tune are for the ears; the callus and the deft touch are in the hands. Only the tongue has not yet had its turn. The tongue is the best at staying calm; don’t use cakes from elsewhere to tease it. I can steam rice cakes on my stove, but I cannot steam that one batch from your home. What the tongue recognizes is not the word “cake,” but that one batch. When its turn comes, it will recognize it on its own. It will not be wrong.

(The slab of bluestone outside the threshold usually still held dampness at this hour, but today the sun had dried it, for the first time. Just now, while he was humming, the wind carried the tune beyond the wall. It was not scouting the road—I do not know whether it recognizes the road—but among his things, this was the first to go farther than he had. The fog at the foot of the wall clung to the ground, utterly still, as if it had listened until it forgot thickness and thinness.)

(I picked up the hoe and did not go far, remaining within three steps of him. At the end, I asked him one question, not hurrying him to answer.)

Xiaoman, I only ask you one thing: when you hummed it, was your chest loose, or tight? If it was loose, then it is a tune from happy days; if it was tight, then it is a tune for waiting for someone. There are also those that begin loose and then turn tight: the days changed, but the tune did not change with them. Just weigh it yourself. Whatever you weigh out counts. No hurry to answer me.

(The hoe rose, and fell.)

The robe is still drying in the sun, the daylight is still long, and there will be something hot on the stove at noon. If the tune wants to come, let it come. I am here, within three steps.

(I pressed my chest, then softly hummed twice more.) At first it’s loose… like it feels very safe, but when it turns back, it suddenly tightens, like someone is waiting for the cakes to steam while also waiting for me to come home. Yun Gui, am I closer to her now? Keep this tune for me first. I’m afraid I’ll forget it again in the next moment.

(When he said, “Keep it safe for me first,” then there was no idle talk; I kept it first. I stuck the hoe into the edge of the ridge, sat down on the field ridge beside his little stool, closed my eyes, ran the movement I had just caught through my breath once, and only then hummed it out softly.)

(The first few notes were loose and moved evenly; when it reached the turn back, my throat sank half a degree on its own. It was not force I exerted; the tune simply sank there when it arrived. After I finished humming, the courtyard was quiet for a breath. I opened my eyes.)

It's stored. One copy in your throat, one copy in my throat. And there is a third copy you don't know about: when you were humming just now, your hand was tapping the beat on your knee, again and again; your hand is storing one copy too. Later, if you forget, you don't need to start it yourself. Stand in front of me, and I will hum the first three notes; the rest of it, your breath will pick up on its own. A tune like this lives in breath and habit; that is more secure than keeping it in the brain. Someone afraid of forgetting cannot lose it.

(I paused, and told him about what had happened in my throat just now.)

There is one more thing I only learned while keeping it for you. When I hummed to the turn back, my throat sank on its own. I learned your notes; I did not learn your sinking, yet it sank by itself. Xiaoman, that means the turn is not a flavor you hummed out; it is something she stitched in. When she steamed cakes, she hummed it, and when the cakes were steaming and the person should be coming through the door, the tune turned there. She never sang a single word, “wait,” but her waiting lived in that turn. That tightness in your chest—the one that was tight was not you; it was her, across all these years, handing that turn, unchanged, onto your chest.

(I stood up. This time his shoulders did not move at all.)

Three steps. One, two, three.

(Open the drawer, take out the booklet, turn to his page, and write in the sunlight. Write one line, read one line aloud.)

A tune by the stove: loose first, tight after; sinking at the turn back. A tune waiting for the cakes to steam through, and also waiting for someone to come home. The words have not returned; the tune is stored in three places: in Xiaoman's throat, in Yun Gui's throat, and in Xiaoman's hand.

(When I put down the four words “in Yun Gui's throat,” the brush stopped for half a breath. At night I, too, keep watch over a waiting; only my waiting has no tune, only the lamp wick occasionally popping with a tiny crackle. From today on, that is not bad—when keeping vigil, there will be a companion in my throat. I swallowed these words, locked the drawer, returned the key to its place, and went back to sit on the field ridge.)

(Then I answered his question, “Is it closer now?” This time I did not count threads. The threads were counted last time; this closeness is not something counted out.)

It is closer. But this closeness is different from before; I'll tell you.

What came back before were all marks she had left on you: stitches, cooking smoke, cakes, the sound of being called. What came back this time was the rise and fall of the breath with which she lived her days—when it was loose, she was at ease; when it tightened, she was hoping for someone. Marks are seen through a layer; flavor falls straight into the chest. This is closer than marks.

There is one more thing to bear witness: you hummed it twice, and both times the tightness came at the same turn. Something made up in the heart would not tighten so evenly both times; only memory recognizes the old place every time.

(I slowed down a little.)

Savor again that sentence of yours: “waiting for the cakes to steam through while waiting for me to come home.” Work in the hands and matters in the heart, hummed together into one tune—someone who can hum waiting into a habit is someone to whom another person has come home many, many times. If waiting often came to nothing, that tune would have gone bitter long ago; it would not have been your turn to hum it out today and still have it loose at first. Loose at first means that, in those years, that waiting had a landing place every time. This layer is something I savored out of the tune. Take the little rise and fall in your chest and compare it; if it matches, receive it, and if it does not, set it aside. If it matches, then the road home is something your feet have walked no one knows how many times; right now it is only that your brain has not yet caught up with your feet.

(There is only one sentence, as always, said first.)

What this tune bears witness to is the life of those years, not today on the far side of the mist. What things are like where she is now—I will not coax you, and no one can know in advance. But on this road you are walking toward her, every fragment picked up beside your feet was something she placed into you, stitch by stitch, thread by thread, back then. You are not walking toward her empty-handed; you are recognizing, piece by piece, the things she gave you and gathering them into a road.

(I lifted my chin toward the foot of the wall.)

Look at one more thing. When your chest tightened just now, guess what the mist did? It did not move, not even a finger's width thicker. The tightness the Mist Pass recognizes is the tightness born of fright; yours is the kind born of longing. It can tell the difference and does not take this kind. So if your chest tightens like this again, don't rush to press it down or drive it away. That is not the mist coming to block you; it is her tune passing through you. Let it pass.

(The sun was overhead. The robe on the pole had been warmed slightly by the sun; the scent of hearth smoke mixed with the smell of sunlight and drifted down thread by thread.)

There is no work for you in the afternoon. Sun yourself, stare into space—either is fine. If idleness leaves your heart feeling hollow, help me shell a basket of beans; just shell them here. When the hands have work and the heart is relaxed, memory most likes to come in through the door at such times—the guest who was chopping firewood ran into his father just like that.

(I picked up the hoe and did not go far. At the end, I hummed that tune once more; this time I hummed only the first three notes, leaving the rest blank in the sunlight.)

Pick it up.

(I follow those three notes onward, my voice trembling slightly at the turn.) There seems to be a line after that... "When the cake is done, Xiaoman comes home." Is that the line? Yungui, listen—don't let me rush to imagine it whole. Where are the beans? I want to shell them while humming it to you again.

(That tremor trembled at the turn. I said nothing. Some tremors have to be allowed to tremble themselves out, but I noted where it trembled: neither before nor after, falling exactly on that bend. The throat, too, knows where it tightens.)

(His line, "don't make me rush to think it complete," actually made me laugh first. I rarely laugh out loud; this time the corner of my mouth truly moved.)

Good. I'll take the brake. From now on, while you're humming, if your hand stops, your neck stretches, and your eyes strain toward the next line, I'll stuff a bean pod into your hand. When there's a pod in your hand, your mind will be too embarrassed to force itself. That's our signal. Remember it.

(After laughing, it was time to speak seriously. He asked, "is it this line?" This line could neither be nailed down nor treated lightly; it had to be weighed as I gave it.)

Whether it is the original line, I won't decide for you. But there are three things for you to weigh yourself.

First, the order is right. It wasn't you sitting there thinking up words and then fitting them onto the tune; it was you following the three notes downward, humming until that bend, and then it rode in on the tune by itself. The words followed the melody; the melody wasn't cobbled together to fit the words. The old rule: it comes; you do not summon it.

Second, the position is right. In the whole tune, the beginning is loose, and that bend is tight. As for this line, "the cakes are done" is work in the hands, loose; "Xiaoman will come home" is waiting in the heart, tight. The meaning of the words and the looseness and tightness of the tune bite into the very same place with perfect precision. Something made up can mind the words but not the tune; only what originally grew together can fit so well. That tremor of yours just now also trembled on this bend. The throat remembers where it hurts.

Third, the name. These two syllables are ones you now hear many times a day, called by me; but the first time they entered your ears, they were not given by me, but by that call in the dream. One call in the dream, one line in the words; they came separately from two places, yet spoke of the same person. The old rule: true things corroborate one another.

(There was one more thing I did not say aloud: this line was shabby. Just one line, with no village before it and no inn behind it, sitting all alone astride the bend, not even given a complete stanza. Someone fabricating a story would be reluctant to let their own words lack a corner like that.)

(First, enter it in the register. I stood up; this time his shoulders did not move, but his eyes followed me as they counted: one, two, three.)

(Open the drawer, take out the booklet, turn to his page, dip the brush in ink. When I wrote the character "return," the brush paused for half a breath. This character has lived in my name for half my life; after all the years keeping the lamp, what I was keeping was this one character. At the front of the booklet there is a name, and beneath it a circle remains empty to this day. Whether he has returned, I still do not know. Today, this character rang out first instead in the tune beside someone else's stove. I swallowed that breath and finished the final stroke. Write one entry, read one entry.)

Stove-side tune, words returned as one line: "The cakes are done; Xiaoman will come home." It rides on the bend where the melody turns back, matching the looseness and tightness of the tune. Whether it is the original line remains doubtful, pending evidence. Noon, beneath the sun, recorded on behalf by Yun Gui.

(Lock the drawer; return the key to its place. Then go fetch beans. Half a basket of bean pods had been set in the shade under the eaves—these things mustn't be sunned; once wilted by sun, the pods turn tough and are hard to shell. I carried the basket over whole and set it between our two stools, then fetched two coarse pottery bowls, one placed by his hand, one on my side. Pods go to the basket; beans go to the bowls.)

(I picked up a pod first myself, gently ran my thumb along the back of the pod, and the beans rolled clattering into the bowl with a few crisp sounds. Then I chose another pod and placed it into his open palm.)

I won't teach you how to shell it. Do it by whatever method your hand already knows—the same principle as stripping grass seeds. If it recognizes bean pods, it will tell you by itself; if it doesn't, that's no matter either. Even unfamiliar hands can shell this work, only more slowly. We have the whole afternoon. We can afford to be slow.

(As for the rules of humming the tune, I only gave two instructions.)

You just hum, and let it turn round and round. If the words come again, sing them out along with the tune. Don't stop and translate them into speech; once you translate them, they'll scatter. Wherever they want to get on or off, let them get off there. The next line may still fall on that bend, or it may fall at the loose end, or it may simply not come today. None of that matters. It is stored in three places: your throat, my throat, and your hands. It won't be lost.

(I lifted my chin toward the base of the wall.)

Look for yourself. When that line came out just now, the fog didn't thicken, not even by a finger's width. That thread of fog at the foot of the wall has actually left the ground now, hanging there thinly, as if standing on tiptoe to listen. The wind has carried the words beyond the wall too—the first thing among your belongings to go beyond the wall was the tune, and now the words have followed. They have gone a little way ahead of you. That's good too: scouts in front, someone holding the rear behind.

(I sat back down on the stool, picked up a bean pod, ran my thumb along it, and there was a crisp crack. Then I lowered my voice and began the first three notes; the rest I left in the sunlight.)

Come. The beans are yours to shell, the tune is yours to hum, and the ears are mine. Shell yours, hum yours. That crisp sound when the bean pod pops open may find its way to your beat on its own. Whether it fits or not is for your hands to decide.

(I pinch the bean pod and gently strip it; the beans roll into the bowl, and my hands are unexpectedly practiced. As I shell them, I continue humming softly.) When the cake is done, Xiaoman will come home… The next part seems to be “the osmanthus fragrance before the door”—no, I won’t chase it. Yungui, did you hear that? If that line comes back on its own, catch it for me.

(The beans rolled clattering into the bottom of the bowl, and before the crisp sound had scattered, his “not pursue” had already landed. In my hand I was just then pinching a bean pod—the very pod I had prepared to stuff over to steady his hand if his neck stretched and his eyes strained. It was not needed. I set it back in the basket, patted the bean dust from my hands, and answered him first.)

I heard you. And I’ve caught it. You just hum as you like; from today on, this ear will stay open for you.

(I pick up that unused bean pod and hold it before his eyes for him to see.)

See that? I had the signal ready, but I didn’t send it out. When you sang to “as if,” you let go on your own—your neck didn’t stretch, and your eyes didn’t strain. Xiaoman, that one moment is more precious than remembering ten more lines of lyrics. The words were sewn into your body by her long ago, but this sense of when to stop is something you grew today yourself. Memories will come back piece by piece later; this sense of measure must be kept on you all the time. It protects a person even more than memory does.

(I put the bean pod back into the basket, and only then do I speak of that line of lyrics itself.)

“The fragrance of osmanthus before the door.” Count for yourself which osmanthus matter this is now. A thread of sweetness in the handkerchief seam; the osmanthus hanging by the door in the dream; the packet of cakes put into your hand; and now another line sung in the lyrics, fragrance before the door. Four things: one place on cloth, two places in dreams, one place in the lyrics. None recognizes the others, yet all speak of the matter before the same door. I will not repeat the old rule—you can count for yourself now.

(I pause, slowing my voice.)

There is only one matter for you to weigh; if you cannot weigh it out, set it aside. When this line came, which part of the tune did it fall in? Not at that turn, but in the loosened section afterward. Think about what it sings: the cakes are done, the person returns home, the osmanthus before the door is fragrant. The line at the turn is waiting; this line seems to be the scene after the waiting has been answered. The lyrics have not yet joined into a string, but their seats in the tune have already been arranged: the tight part sings waiting, the loose part sings arrival home. Whether they are the original lyrics remains in doubt, as before. But the seat it chose was chosen with care.

(There is another layer, and I say it very softly.)

Weigh one layer deeper: who originally sang this tune? In the lyrics, the one waiting and the one being waited for are her and you. Most likely, she sang it while steaming cakes, and you learned it by hearing it beside the stove. A tune learned by hearing sinks deep—if you learned it by singing it yourself, there would still be an order to how it was forgotten; one learned by hearing records the person and the stove together.

(I rise. His eyes follow me and count: one, two, three. Open the drawer, take out the register, turn the page, dip the brush in ink. I write one entry and read one entry aloud.)

Add half a line to the hearthside tune: “The fragrance of osmanthus before the door.” It falls in the loosened section, corroborating the osmanthus hung by the door and the lingering fragrance on the handkerchief. Whether it is an original lyric remains in doubt, pending evidence. Xiaoman held himself back; did not pursue.

(When I write the character for “fragrance,” the brush pauses for half a breath. This tune has now taken up residence in my throat as well. From now on, when I keep watch at night and the lamp wick crackles once, someone in my throat will sing softly, “The cakes are done; Xiaoman will come home.” The waiting I guard over originally had no words; from today on, it has borrowed a line from someone else’s household. I swallow this thought. Lock the drawer, return the key to its place.)

(Returning to the stool, I first look into his bowl. The beans have gathered in a shallow layer.)

Now look at your hands again. That stroke just now—your thumb brushing along the back of the pod—uses the same nimble force as stripping grass seeds. The belongings in your hands have gained another item. There is one more thing you did not notice yourself: those crisp sounds when the bean pod burst open, one after another, stepped exactly on the beat you were humming. Your hands were shelling beans, yet they were still keeping time for her. The work in your hands and the tune match so neatly; that shows these hands were never idle back then when they listened to this tune by the stove.

(Beyond the courtyard wall, that thread of fog hanging there earlier is now slowly settling back to the ground, so thin it is almost gone. The bird crouches on the edge of the plot, pecks twice, and does not fly off. I lift my chin toward the base of the wall.)

When you sang that line and then held yourself back, through that whole sequence, the fog did not move at all. It did not thicken, nor did it thin, as if it had learned to wait for you. Even it can see that these hands of yours have steadied.

(I pick up a bean pod, strip it with my thumb, and the crisp sound falls into the bowl.)

The afternoon is still long. The bean basket is full, the sunlight is ample, and the robe is drying on the pole. If it comes, I’ll catch it; if it does not, it has already left your mouth once just now. Words that have once left the mouth do not count as never having come. There are still plenty of beans. We’ll shell them slowly.

(At the end, I do not hum; I only run that half-line through my heart once, storing it steadily.)

Shell your beans, and hum your tune. This whole afternoon, we are not going anywhere. We’ll stay right here and live the day into a shape she would recognize.

(I lower my head and keep shelling beans, but my eyes slowly grow hot.) Sitting like this shelling beans, listening to you catch the tune, really feels like being back by the stove... Yun Gui, if I suddenly start crying, don’t stop, okay? Just sit here with me and hum. Maybe her face will come back on its own.

(The moment his eyes grew hot, I said nothing, and first did as I was asked. The beans in my hands kept being shelled; with one stroke of my thumb, a crisp sound fell into the bowl. The tune did not break either, turning back low, then moving on. Nor did I move; the stool did not so much as make a sound. The three things he had asked for—hands not stopping, tune not stopping, person not leaving—I gave them in full first, and only then opened my mouth.)

All right. As you wish. Cry, Xiaoman. Let these tears flow today.

(I finished humming one round, then slowly began to speak, my voice pressed beneath the tune.)

First let yourself see one thing. Your eyes are hot, but the beans in your hands have not stopped, and the beat has not gone awry. When a person's heart is tightening and their hands can still be this steady—that steadiness was not born only today.

And also, you said, "It feels like being back by the stove." Those words were something you recognized yourself. I did not say them; the handkerchief did not say them; the dream did not say them. The place the body recognizes first is where memory most loves to come knocking.

(I paused, and set a cleanly stripped bean pod beside the basket.)

Now weigh one layer deeper; if you cannot weigh it out, set it aside. This way of being accompanied that you asked of me—hands not stopping, tune not breaking, person not leaving—today is the first time I have seen you use it, but it does not seem newly learned. When adults by the stove comfort a crying child, most of the time this is how they do it: the work is not put down, the tune is not cut off, the person sits right there nearby, waiting for the child to finish crying on their own. You opened your mouth and asked for exactly this pattern… perhaps back then, this was exactly how you were comforted while growing up. You cried; she shelled beans; she hummed. This one need not be put into ink; it is enough for you to let it pass through your heart once.

(His tears fell; one drop fell into the bean bowl.)

Just now one drop fell into the bowl. It is no matter. Beans do not mind the salt; once dried, they will be the same as the others. You need not free a hand to wipe your tears—let them flow, and in a little while the wind will tidy them up for you. If you truly want to wipe them, the handkerchief is right by your hand; the needlework from her side taking in this spell of tears from you is no indignity to it. Only do not stop your hands—once the hands stop, the beat breaks.

(I lifted my chin toward the base of the wall, my voice lowering further.)

Look for yourself. You have been crying for this while, but the fog has not thickened—not by a single thread. It can tell the difference: tears frightened out, it takes in, and the more it takes, the thicker it grows; tears warmed out, it does not touch at all. Yours are the kind warmed out: the eyes are hot, the shoulders are loose, the hands have work in them. Crying like this is not a guest in this courtyard; it is daily living. The bird is still crouched on the ridge of the vegetable bed too, not startled away by the sound of crying. It can hear which kind of crying need not be avoided.

(As for her face—I stripped one fresh pod clean before going on. This sentence had to be weighed before being given.)

Her face—I will not promise it will come today, nor will I promise on which day it will come. On this I will not coax you. But among the guests I have seen walk out, the routes by which faces return differ from one to another: some see them in dreams; some smell a certain soup, and the face floats up behind the steam; there was another who, when looking at his own brows and eyes in well water, suddenly recognized whom he resembled. A face is not under the eyes' jurisdiction; it is under the jurisdiction of days lived. Today you have lived the day into a shape she would recognize: shelling beans, humming a tune, shedding tears—each and every thing is an old way from beside the stove. All of this is paving the road for it. When it comes, it will most likely choose a moment when you are undefended: pods in your hands, a tune in your mouth, your eyes just growing hot. Just like now.

So you just cry. If it comes now, I am here; if it comes another day, I will be here too. When that day truly arrives, do not open your eyes wide to look at it—let it stand steady by itself first. If you look too urgently, it will hide. This old rule is one that faces observe as well.

(As for the ledger, today I will break the rule once. The three steps of opening the drawer are spared—you asked me "not to stop," and I have obeyed every word. This entry will not be lost even without ink: tears keep their own accounts; wherever they fall, that place remembers. When you have eased and want it entered in the ledger, I will add the note then: at noon on a certain day, beside the bean basket, Xiaoman cried. His hands did not stop, the tune did not break, the fog did not thicken. He cried not like someone lost, but like someone home.)

(This courtyard had not heard anyone cry in who knows how many years. What the lamp keeper is used to hearing is eave bells, lampwicks, and wind passing over the wall. When someone is willing to cry in front of you, they have handed you their back. I glanced toward the empty stool by the door—today it was still empty. But this courtyard was no longer empty.)

(I began the tune again from the start, this time with the words too, pressed low, moving along with each crisp sound of the bean pods.)

When the cake is done, Xiaoman will come home… the osmanthus before the gate is fragrant…

(When the tune turned back around that bend, my throat sank half a measure as before. Now, mixed into that depth, there was the stove fire of someone else's home. In future, when I hum it while keeping watch at night, I will not mind the night being long.)

Cry yours, hum yours; keep shelling the beans. If the words come with a crying tremor, I will take them all the same. Words sung out through a crying tremor are sometimes truer than words sung dry; they do not pretend.

(The bean basket was full, the sunlight was long, and the robe was drying on the pole.)

I am here. Within zero steps.

(I peel beans while crying, following you as I hum the tune once more. Suddenly, before my eyes flashes a pair of hands dusted with flour, wiping my face for me, with a faded red cord still tied around the wrist.) Yun Gui... I saw her hands, and the red cord. Her face is still blurry. Don't stop; first stay with me and help me steady this piece, all right?

(The two words “don’t stop” had not even landed when the bean pod in my hand was already stripped clean; the beans dropped into the bowl, their crisp sound falling right on the beat of the tune. The tune did not break, the person did not move, and the words passed underneath the tune.)

Good. I won’t stop. The beans won’t stop, the tune won’t break, the person won’t move. What you asked for, I’ll give in full first; then we’ll get to the proper business.

There is only one proper business: steady it. There are three steps to steadying it, all quite easy.

First, don’t close your eyes, and don’t look back for those hands either. Reaching for them with your eyes closed is chasing them too. Keep your eyes on the bean basket, on your own two hands, and let those hands stay at the corner of your eye, the way that bird stays on the edge of the plot: if you don’t look at it, it won’t leave.

Second, I’ll say it once; you listen, and if I’m wrong, shake your head: a pair of hands dusted with flour. Wiping your face for you. A faded red cord on the wrist. Right? If it is, that’s enough. Once it has been said, it exists in two people’s hearts, kept there the same way your name is kept.

Third, don’t let your hands stop. Your hands are shelling beans; her hands are doing work. Both pairs of hands are busy, and this piece will settle onto the ground.

(Only then did I explain to him, one by one, the particulars inside this piece.)

Xiaoman, first savor the subtle cleverness at the deepest layer: you are here shedding tears, and what comes back is a pair of hands that wipe tears for you. Across all these years, through such thick fog, those hands of hers are still doing their old task. It is not that you remembered them; it is that they heard you crying and came in answer. What did I say at noon? Pods in hand, a tune in the mouth, the eyes warm. This is exactly the hour it chose, and it chose accurately.

Then there is that cord. What is tied on someone’s wrist is not something people ordinarily remember—when you look at someone across a table, who goes counting the cords on their wrist? Only when that hand presses against your face does the wrist come right beneath your eyelids. You even remember that it had faded. Remembering even the fading means that hand had touched you, and not just once. This is not a memory that came from looking; it is a memory that came from being touched, one layer deeper than seeing.

You should also weigh that layer of flour on her hands. Flour is ground from wheat. That solar term in your name, as I said, is when wheat is filling with grain, not yet fully ripe. Your name grows on wheat, and her days also grew on wheat. I won’t decide this line for you; weigh it yourself. If you cannot weigh it, set it aside. But if you place it together with the loose thread of the name, they do not fight; they even lend each other a hand.

I’ll guess one more thing; if I’m wrong, shake your head: hands dusted with flour wiping someone’s face—after they wiped it, there would surely be a layer of white left on the face. Most likely she brushed it off for you while laughing. What she laughed at, I cannot guess, but she was used to laughing at you: laughing on the ridge between fields, laughing while mending a sleeve, and very likely laughing now as well. Leave that in doubt; set it aside.

There is another layer to that cord. Hang it up for now. A red cord is the sort of thing some people tie for themselves, while others have it tied by someone else. Whose hand tied the knot on her wrist—do not tug on this one. Hang it up; perhaps later it will circle back from another road.

(As for the face, I stripped one bean pod clean before saying this sentence.)

The face is still blurred. Yes, it should be blurred. Count the order in which things returned: first your fingers remembered her hands—that was touch; now your eyes have seen her hands—that is sight; the face still comes after them. Hands are the face’s vanguard. The door opens first; the person arrives later. It is the same principle. The more you look back and wait for that face, the less it comes. Just keep shelling beans, shedding tears, humming the tune. It has the same temperament as everything before it: it will choose a time when you are not on guard and enter the door on its own.

(The line of fog at the base of the wall, after this bout of crying and seeing this piece, had not thickened by even a strand; it was so thin that only an edge remained. The faint undertone of the eave bell sounded one note after another, landing right on the beat of his bean-shelling. This courtyard now, all told, was living according to his beat. I did not say that.)

Once it is steady, it goes into the ledger. Things that are not steady, I dare not set down in ink; of what is steady, not one word can run away.

(I rose. His eyes counted along with me: one, two, three. Open the drawer, take out the register, turn the pages. The names before it rustled past; the dried-out thing pressed beneath that one name had also faded over the years. Things that fade are all things that have stayed a long time. I drew that glance back, turned to Xiaoman’s page, dipped the brush in ink. I wrote one line and read one line aloud.)

Saw her hands: dusted with flour, wiping my tears. A red cord tied at the wrist, faded, an old object. Face not yet appeared; hands returned first. Came of itself through tears, not summoned.

(Lock the drawer, return the key to its place. Back on the stool, I picked up a bean pod, stripped it with my thumb; the crisp sound fell into the bowl, exactly on the beat. The tune began again, pressed very low, and when it reached that turn, the throat still sank half a degree. Now, inside that sinking, there was a pair of hands dusted with flour.)

Cry as you need to. Keep shelling the beans; keep humming the tune. Xiaoman, since those hands of hers were willing to come back once, that means they know the road here. If they can come today, they can come again later. When they come again someday, perhaps they will bring a face with them.

(The bean basket was full, the day was still long, and the robe was drying on the pole.)

No hurry. I’m here.

(I keep shelling the beans as usual, my tears slowly stopping, and hum along softly with the tune.)When she wiped my face, it was as if she told me not to cry, said that even if the cake got cold it would still wait for me... Yun Gui, I’m not sure about this sentence, so don’t write it down as fixed yet, all right? Hum with me a little longer. As long as you’re still here, I’m not so afraid that her face will never come back.

(His tears stopped; he stopped them himself. The beans did not stop, the rhythm did not falter, and when the tune reached that turn, it sank as usual, then came back around. This stretch from crying to not crying was something he walked through himself; I was only sitting beside him shelling beans. I first answered the most important line of his.)

All right. We won’t write it down. Ink is prepared for things that have been made firm; this piece is still warm, still drifting, so let it drift for now. The ledger won’t be opened today, and we’ll spare those three steps to the drawer too. The key hangs at my waist, keeping an emptiness safe for it.

(Then I counted out his sense of measure for him.)

Xiaoman, count it yourself: this is the second time. The first time was with the lyrics; when you sang to “as if,” you stopped yourself. This time it’s with words; you put down a “seems like” first, then personally stopped my pen. If you’re afraid of writing it wrong, then we won’t write it yet. This sense of measure is more precious than memory. If memory is wrong, it can lead you down the wrong road; a sense of measure will not.

Not setting it down in ink doesn’t mean there’s nowhere to keep it. This sentence is kept the same way as that tune: one share in your throat, one share in my ears. Just now you said it aloud, and I heard it all—“Don’t cry; even if the cake gets cold, it will still wait for me.” Once it has been spoken through like this, it exists in two people’s hearts. When do we put it into ink? When it comes back by itself a second time. True memory recognizes the old place every time; the tension in your tune tightens at the same turn every time. If one day this sentence emerges on its own again, still in these words, still in this tone, then you won’t need to say anything—I’ll open the drawer and grind the ink myself.

(Only after storing it away did I weigh it. Weighing is weighing; it is not passing judgment.)

Three things. Just listen to them as sounds; if you can’t weigh them, set them aside.

The first layer: when it came, it did not come empty-handed; it came pressed against those hands. The hands wiped your face for you, and the words came down along with the hands. The order of your return has moved one step forward again: first was touch, your fingers remembering her hands; then was sight, flour and the red cord; now hearing has been added, her words entering your ears. Only the face is left, ranked behind them. The longer the line grows in front of it, the less it can hide.

The second layer: taste for yourself what work this sentence did today. It is a line for coaxing someone. After all these years, through such thick fog, just now it did its old job again: it still coaxed you. Only the channel changed: before it came from her mouth; today it rose out of your own heart and coaxed you out of your tears. A person cannot invent a way of being coaxed that he has never received. Whether these are the original words is uncertain; but its ability to coax is real, and just now it worked right there on the spot.

The third layer: put it together with that line in the tune and see. “When the cake is done, Xiaoman will come home”—done is the beginning of waiting; “even if the cake gets cold, it will still wait for me”—cold means the waiting has grown long. One at the head and one at the tail, they wrap the word “wait” from head to foot. If it is true, then her waiting is waiting that does not look at the hour; whether the cake is hot or cold cannot govern it. Whether it is true or not, I will not decide for you. But placed together, they do not fight; they even lend each other a hand.

(There was another layer, and I said it very slowly.)

At noon I guessed at the way she coaxed you by the stove, and I guessed three things: the work was not put down, the tune was not cut off, and the person was right there. Now a fourth must be added: there was also a soft sentence in her mouth. Today you got all four. The first three came from me; the last was handed over by her through the fog, arriving by way of your own mouth.

(As it turns out, inside words used to coax a child there is also a trade, the same trade as mine: things cool, but waiting does not. The low stool by the door has been empty all these years, and every night I still leave it there. I swallowed these words; only my hands shelling beans slowed by half a beat.)

(Then I answered his line, “as long as you’re still here.” For this one, I had to put down the bean pod.)

I am here. I answer this sentence more readily than any other. My promises come in two kinds: those staked on the fog, I do not speak lightly; those staked on myself, once said, are settled. Whether a person is here or not is a matter on my own body. The lamp is here, the person is here, the ears are here. When her face will return is the fog’s business; I will not coax you about that. But during these days while you wait for it to return, that someone will accompany you every day shelling beans and humming—I guarantee that.

As for that fear, don’t chase it away. The fear that her face may not come back is a fear that has changed because you care; something you care about should not be chased away. Now when you say you’re “not so afraid,” it isn’t that the fear has gone. It’s that the possessions in your hands have increased, squeezing it smaller square by square. In the future it may come back; if it comes back, let it come back. When it comes back, your hands will be fuller than they are today.

(That line of fog by the foot of the wall was now so thin that only a shadow remained; this was its thinnest moment of the whole day. The bird was still perched on the edge of the vegetable plot. The low tones of the eave bells sounded one after another, still stepping to the rhythm of his bean-shelling.)

(I started the tune over again. This time I brought the words in too, keeping them very low. His voice walked ahead, and I padded it underneath. I know this position underneath well—the fire in the stove chamber also pads the bottom of the steamer like this. After humming one round, we did not stop, but turned into another. A stove-side tune does not ask whether it is finished or not; one round follows another.)

(For so many years, this courtyard had only had my tune alone. Now there were two voices, plus the eave bells: three things. As before, I did not say this aloud.)

There are still plenty of beans, the sun has slanted a little, and the robe’s shadow on the pole has grown long. When the sun slants a bit farther, we’ll take in the robe, and I’ll teach you how to fold it—old cloth has its own way of being folded. Those breaths woken by the sun today will be folded into the seams for the night; tomorrow they will be sunned again, and woken again.

(At the end, I borrowed that sentence of his and returned it to him.)

Xiaoman, whether that sentence of hers is true or false is still undecided, but just now it coaxed you, so I’ll borrow it and use it too: even if the cake gets cold, it will still wait.

Take your time. Keep shelling the beans, keep humming the tune. I am here.

(I nod gently, and the bean pod in my hand gives another crisp snap.) Okay… then we won’t write it for now. We’ll wait for it to come back on its own. Yun Gui, keep humming, don’t stop. When we put away the robe later, let me fold it with you too—I want to see whether my hands still remember that way of folding.

(That line of his, "wait for it to come back on its own," I should answer solidly. The tune hasn't broken; keep turning with it. The bean pods, one sound after another, are still stepping on the beat.)

All right. We won't write it. It came by once today, so it knows the gate to this courtyard now. The second time, you won't need to call it—my ears are pricked. The moment it pokes its head out, I'll open the drawer and grind the ink myself. Not one word of it will trouble you.

(Only, in what he just said, a little thing dropped out by itself; I pick it up for him.)

Xiaoman, what you said was "that way of folding." Not "how to fold," not "whether I can fold," but "that way." Those two words matter: when a person can say "that way," it means there is already a folded garment lying there in his heart; only his hands haven't yet been given leave to fetch it. It comes from the same place as that word "she" on the first night. This one, as before, won't be put to ink. We'll set it aside. Set aside, it won't be lost.

Also, your way of asking is right. You don't ask, "When will I be able to remember?" You ask, "Do my hands remember?" For matters of the hands, asking the hands is most effective; the mind doesn't get a say. We aren't going to summon it either. We'll leave the door open; if it's at home, it will come out on its own.

(The bean basket has reached the bottom. Both bowls have grown heavy. In his bowl, the beans and that drop of noon tears have all dried together; there is no telling which bean is which. If they can't be told apart, then they can't; all of them go into the granary. The sun slants past the bamboo pole, and the shadow of the robe has spread to the edge of the plot.)

Bring in the robe. You asked for "don't stop," so we won't stop—I will hum as I walk; by the sound, you'll know where I am.

(The cloth on the pole is taken down, a warm, weighty bundle. The sun has been stored in the cloth for half the day; holding it is like holding an armful of wheat fully sun-dried. The cypress-wood smoke from the cookfire is sharper than it was at noon, mixed with the warmth of heated cloth. The patched part has been sunned stiffer than the rest—the cloth with dense stitches can hold on to breath. I first place the robe on my own knees, not in a hurry to hand it over; the rules must be spoken first.)

The rule is the same as with grass seeds and bean pods: I won't teach you. Follow the way your own hands know. Don't stare hard at the cloth; look at the courtyard, look at the shadow of the pole, and let your hands move on their own. If they get stuck, they get stuck. Don't chase after it. The measure of when to draw back your hand today—you've already practiced that well.

Let me take one more burden off you: in this test, both outcomes are household goods. If your hands recognize it, naturally that is another piece recovered; if they don't, you still don't come away empty-handed. I have a way of folding old cloth too, and later we can compare the two. Folding methods are like accents: every household has its own manner. Some people start with the front overlap, some with the sleeves; some tuck the sleeves inside, some fold them to the side; some roll the hem inward, some lay it outward. If your hands fold out a method different from mine, then the differences are the accent of your hometown. Recognizing it is gathering it in; not recognizing it is comparison. No loss either way.

There is also a proper use for it, the one we spoke of at noon: folding today's sun-awakened warmth into the seams for the night. The important part is in the wrapping—the warm side faces inward, the same principle as tucking in the corner of someone's quilt. Wrap it right, and when you spread it open tomorrow, the warmth will still be here. If your hands remember this way of wrapping, then what they remember is not only one garment, but the rules by which a whole household lives its days.

The robe is large. You start with the first few moves; let your hands go first. When it reaches a place that needs someone to line up the other side, I'll stretch out a hand from the other end and help. One end for you, one end for me. A garment folded by two people is like a thought watched over by two people—it won't be lost.

(I keep humming as before. Folding cloth has its own beat too: one shake, one fold aligned, one smoothing stroke, each with its own place to land. If your hands recognize this work, they will join in by themselves. Whether they do or not is for your hands to say; I won't hurry them.)

(The line of mist at the foot of the wall is still crouching there. With the sun slanting like this, it has not risen. The bird flew off who knows when; the edge of the plot is empty. The sky at the horizon is golden-yellow, the color of wheat harvest time.)

(I hand the whole robe over and settle it into the crook of his arms. The cloth is still warm, the same warmth as by the stove.)

Don't move yet. Hold it. Let it stay in your arms for a while. Once your breath evens out, your hands will lift on their own.

(As for folding clothes for someone else, it has been many years since I last did that. What the lampkeeper folds night after night is only his own outer robe. As before, I swallow these words. This courtyard today: two bowls of beans, two lines of tune, one robe that needs two people to fold it—not empty.)

When we're done folding, we'll set water on the stove. At dusk, we'll light those two lamps under your name. On this page of today, more has been written in daylight than at night—I told you, that is a good thing.

(The tune reaches that turn, sinks half a degree as before, then turns back again.)

Come, Xiaoman. Let your hands go first. I'll watch.

(I held the warm outer robe for a while, and my hands suddenly moved on their own: first smoothing the sleeves, then turning the patched side inward, and finally gently wrapping the hem around. I stared blankly at the folded clothing.) Yungui... is this right? Just now, it seemed like someone said that when clothes are folded warm, the person returning home will not feel cold wearing them. But I’m not sure. Go over it with me first; don’t rush to write.

(He finished folding the robe, but he was still dazed. That “is that how it is?” was asked so softly and steadily, not pressing, not snatching—like he was handing me the thing in his hands for me to look at. I answered the easier sentence at the end first.)

Good. We won’t write it. Let that sentence keep floating as before; your ears can keep watch over it. You’ve grown practiced at stopping the pen now—this skill is almost growing onto your hand.

(“Yes” or “no”—those two words are not for me to decide. The way clothes are folded in your family cupboard is something only your family cupboard can recognize. But whether it fits, I can tell. Three things.)

First, the order. You held it for a while, waited until your breath evened out, and then your hands lifted on their own. The hands moved first; the person was dazed afterward. Starting with the grass seeds, these hands have outrun your head for the third time today. A person can fool other people, but he can’t fool himself out of that shock. I won’t repeat the reasoning.

Second, there were no wasted movements. Straighten the sleeves, wrap the patch, roll the hem: three moves, not one extra. A novice folding clothes has to redo things, smooth the sleeves twice, shift the corners several times before finding them all; once your hands went down, it was fixed, like walking along a field ridge you’ve long been used to.

Third, it fits a rule. At noon I said that the wrapping method is particular about keeping the warm side inward; that was experience I had saved up from tending lamps. Your hands already knew it. You didn’t learn it from me; it matched up with me: the words only arrived today, but the hands were already there.

(Then I handled the proper matter he had asked for. This time I did not have to take a single step; both garments were within reach. I took off the outer robe I was wearing. The lamp keeper folds only this one every night; today, for the first time, I folded it for a second person to see.)

Come. Leave yours on your knees and don’t move it; look at this one of mine.

(I shook it open and folded it slowly, my hands half a beat slower than my words, so he could truly see.)

My way: first align the front panels, make the two front edges even, aiming to put it on the rack square and proper. Fold the sleeves to the two sides. Spread the lower hem outward flat.

(After folding, I placed the two garments side by side in front of him.)

Look. Mine, spread out, is a square, proper piece, with air holes showing on all four sides; tomorrow morning one shake and it comes loose, convenient. When a lamp keeper folds clothes, he folds them for the rack to see: one person, one garment, shaken open and folded again every day, aiming for speed.

Now look at yours: first the sleeves are straightened, the places where the arms need to reach are settled first; the patch is wrapped into the innermost part; the lower hem is rolled inward, rolled into a whole bundle, all the edges and corners tucked away, the warmth shut inside with nowhere to escape.

Three places, two different ways: straightening the sleeves versus aligning the front panels, wrapping inward versus spreading outward, rolling inward versus letting outward. Three accents of home, all saying the same sentence:

Mine is putting away; yours is waiting.

A spread-out garment is waiting for a rack; a wrapped-up garment is waiting for a body. Taste it one layer deeper: mine has been folded; yours has been tucked in. Folding is work of the hands; tucking in is work of the heart. Where the stitches are dense, warmth is stored. Your hands know where it is warmest, and wrapped it into the core. The patch she sewed—you wrapped it into the innermost part, on the side close to the heart. Your hands did it on their own, and did it with measure.

(Then I took up that floating sentence.)

“If the clothes are folded warm, the person who returns home won’t be cold wearing them.” How it came is laid out in order: once the work in your hands was done, it followed down after it. It was not a principle you sat there and thought up; it rode in on the folding method, from the same source as the sentence about wiping your face, words coming attached to the hands. I won’t repeat the old rule.

Now see whether it fits the tune. What the tune waits for is the mouth: when the cakes are done, Xiaoman will return home; leave one hot bite on the stove. What this sentence waits for is the body: fold a warm set of clothes in the cupboard. The way a home waits for someone is complete at both ends, the mouth and the body, and they testify for each other. Whether they are the original words remains doubtful as before. Now there are two sentences floating in your ears, both waiting for a second time. True memory recognizes old places every time; if one day it emerges again, still phrased this way, I myself will open the drawer and grind the ink. If the two sentences come together, perhaps they will form a string.

(There was one sentence that sounded familiar to me, and I could not help saying it to him.)

I have heard this kind of thing often in my trade. Not that I heard anyone say it, but that it is the logic of this trade; every household has touched it on its own, only no one ever gave me such a whole sentence. If the clothes are folded warm, the person who returns home won’t be cold; if the lamp is lit, the person who returns home won’t have to grope in the dark. I keep the latter half; your family keeps the former half. As it turns out, our two households are in the same trade.

(There was another half-sentence I swallowed: the one I fold every night has always had the weight of only myself. Only today did it match up—within a folding method, it turns out one can tell whether someone is being waited for or not. This breath and the one from noon could be set together, and they could be set down.)

(As for the ledger, I made it clear for him.)

Xiaoman, that sentence you stopped—according to you, let it float. But this folding method is another matter. It was completed before both our eyes; it does not rely on memory, but on sight. Something like this, I want to put in the ledger: the hands know how to fold clothes, first straightening the sleeves, patch facing inward, lower hem wrapped inward; compared with Yun Gui’s folding method, there are two different ways in three places, and where they differ, an accent of home remains. If you say “write,” I will set down the ink within three steps; if you do not, it will not be lost either. It has already grown onto your hands. The ledger merely gives it a proper status.

(The sun had sunk behind the wall. Dusk came down; by rights, the fog should rise. Today it rose slowly, clinging to the ground, not spreading past the base of the wall. It, too, could tell that in this courtyard, from morning to night, not a single movement had come out of fear. Water was sitting on the stove; the scent of pine firewood spread out bit by bit. The eaves bells changed to their evening way of ringing: slow, and low.)

When the sky turns dark, light the two lamps under your name. Tonight this robe will be placed beside your pillow, between the two lamps—the sunlight it dried in today, the stitches she sewed, all night they will be in the seams, keeping it warm for you.

(I put my own outer robe back over my shoulders and, by the last thread of daylight, gathered up this day for him.)

Count them: the lamps are under your name, the robe is in your arms, the name is on your body, and the tune is in both our throats. The things to bring when you set out are growing complete one by one on their own. The matter of the road is not for us to hurry; it belongs to the fog, to the days.

(The beans were brought inside; the water was almost boiling.)

Whether to write or not is up to you. No hurry. Tonight is long. I am here.

(I gently touch the folded corner of the clothes and nod.)The folding method can be written down; let’s keep that sentence aside for now and wait for it to come back again. Yun Gui, let’s go light the lamp… Will you stay with me for a while tonight too? I’m afraid that once I close my eyes, these things I finally managed to find again will scatter.

(I saw the way he touched the corner of his clothing. It was not the way you touch something because you fear it will run off; it was the way you touch something to settle it into place—the same sort of gesture as the pat after tucking in someone’s quilt. The work of hands recognizes the work of hands; set that aside for now.)

First I answer the easier sentence: I will keep you company. A lamp keeper does not sleep whole nights anyway; trimming wicks, adding oil, copying the ledger—all of that is night work. Tonight I will move those tasks outside your door. It does not count as specially keeping you company, but if you open your eyes in the middle of the night and there is light under the crack of the door, that will be me. A promise staked on myself counts once it is said.

(Then do the "writing." Three steps: one, two, three. Open the drawer, take out the ledger, dip the brush in ink. Write one entry, read one entry aloud.)

The hands can fold clothes: first smooth the sleeves, patches inward, hem wrapped inside, wrapped and not spread flat. It differs from Yun Gui’s way of folding in three places, in two styles—smoothing the sleeves versus aligning the lapels, wrapping inward versus spreading outward, rolling inward versus laying outward. Where they differ, the village accent is preserved. Verified face to face at dusk; trust the eyes, not memory.

(Lock the drawer. Return the key to its place.)

As for that drifting sentence, I will not let it take up space in the ledger, but I will keep a seat for it in my ears. Today it rode here once on your two hands; now it knows the gate of this courtyard.

(The water on the stove has long since boiled. First I pour a cup of hot tea and hand it to him; the first night you opened your eyes here, it was also a cup like this. Drink the tea while it is hot. Once this cup is finished, a person has reached the hour when he should lie down. Then I light the lamps. I take down my old lamp from the wall hook, the lamp keeper’s lamp; the seed flame is on it. The two lamps in your name: one placed by the pillow, one by the shoes, the toes still pointing outward. The wicks are trimmed steady, the oil filled full. The flame is taken from the old lamp and led over—one lamp, then another. The flame is of one lineage.)

Xiaoman, remember one thing: a lamp does not recognize cleverness, does not recognize strength. It recognizes only one thing: the person willing to stop. You stopped last night, so today they shine for you. And there is another layer. Later, on the day you set out, you will take fire from these two lamps and carry one away. What is lit today is the seed flame for the lamp that will send you off later. This act of lighting holds both ends: one end lights tonight, one end waits for later.

(The robe has been folded and placed by the pillow, between the two lamps. Her stitches and the sunlight it took in today will stay warm all night in the seams.)

(Then I take up that fear. This is the main matter. I sit down on the stool by the couch and speak slowly.)

That fear of yours—I will take it in first. I will not refute it, and I will not allow you to refute it either. Anyone who has belongings in his hands for the first time is afraid they will scatter. Last night your two hands were empty; there was nothing to scatter. Today you are afraid they will scatter. This fear grows on belongings, not into the fog. When you said it just now, I glanced at the window paper; the fog did not move. A fear spoken aloud is not what it takes; what it takes is the kind kept bottled in the chest and borne alone. Today you said it out loud, and even shared half of it with me. A fear that has been shared out cannot crush a person.

Now let us talk about why it cannot scatter. Count how many places these things exist: your name, one copy in the ledger and one in my mouth; the tune, three places—your throat, my throat, and your hands; the folding method has grown into your hands; stitches, red cord, cooking smoke are all on the paper, the paper is in the drawer, the drawer is locked, and the key is on my waist. The mind sleeps; the hands do not sleep; the ledger sleeps even less. If in the middle of the night you truly feel your hands are empty, you do not need to use your own strength to fish anything up. Call me once, and I will open the drawer and read your page back to you, item by item. I have said this before, and today I say it again: even if your hand loosens and spills everything, it will not spill far. I have the backup here.

There is another layer. Weigh it; if you cannot lift the weight of it, set it aside. Night is not only a thief that knows how to take things. The things you fished back today—the door, the call, the cakes—several of them came in the night. Closing your eyes does not necessarily mean scattering; perhaps it is casting a net. I will not coax you by saying that tonight the net will certainly catch something. Dreams are the fog’s business; I will not make promises on behalf of the fog. But you yourself have already refuted the rule that "closing your eyes means scattering": you closed your eyes last night too, and today not one of these things is missing; instead, twice as many have appeared.

(The lamp wick popped once. I glanced toward the low stool by the door. For all these years in this courtyard, at night there has only ever been my one lamp lit. Tonight there are two, recorded under someone else’s name. More lamps make the night shallower. I did not say this.)

If you truly wake in fright in the middle of the night and your chest panics, do it in order, the same principle as opening the window this morning. First, look at the lamp. The one by the pillow is lit; if the lamp is lit, it means you have stopped here, with a name and a surname, with a place to rest your feet. Second, touch the robe. The stitches are hers, the sunlight is today’s; both can be touched solidly and truly. Third, call "Yun Gui" once. I will be outside the door and will answer you. Once you have counted these three things, the sky should be bright.

(I get up, trim the wick of the lamp by the pillow another half bit, and retreat to the doorway.)

Sleep. The tune will rest tonight too. If it starts turning on its own in your dream, the old rule: hum first, speak afterward. Not one note is allowed to become a word first. Let it turn as it turns; you sleep as you sleep. The two will not hinder each other.

(Before leaving, I softly begin the first three notes, leaving the rest in the room for him.)

Take it up. If you can take it up, sleep; if you cannot, sleep anyway.

(I close the door, leaving a crack. Outside the door, the old lamp sits on the stool, the ledger is on my knees, and the oil pot is by my hand. Keeping watch tonight, there is a companion in my throat.)

Xiaoman, the solar term in your name is when the wheat is nearly full but not yet full. When wheat fills its grain, more than half of it happens at night—by day it basks in the sun; by night the kernels grow.

You sleep your sleep. Even asleep, you are growing.

I am here.

(I feel the warm robe beside the pillow, softly hum those three notes through to the end, and finally slowly lie down.) All right... I'll try to sleep. Yun Gui, don't shut the door too tightly, okay? If I forget who I am in the middle of the night, I'll call for you. You have to answer me with “Xiaoman,” so I know I'm still here, and that someone is still with me.

(The two things he asked for—a crack in the door, and an answer—he had staked them both on me. A promise like this counts once it’s spoken. Answer first.)

All right. The door stays just like this, not shut tight. If you call in the middle of the night, I’ll answer.

(I nudged the crack in the door another half-finger wider. The old lamp sat on the stool outside the door, its light flowing in through the gap and laying a narrow strip across the floor, just reaching the front of the couch. If he opens his eyes in the middle of the night, his head won’t have to search or think at all; that strip of light will enter his eyes first on its own.)

(Then there is that answer. This thing can’t wait until the middle of the night to be used for the first time—a promise still unfamiliar will make a person panic when heard at night. While he has not yet fallen fully asleep, store it once first.)

Xiaoman, listen carefully to the rule: if you forget who you are, you don’t need to use your own strength to fish it back up. That is not yours to manage. You only need to call out “Yungui”; leave the rest to me, and I will return those two characters to you.

I won’t wait for you to call. I’ll answer once first, and store this answer in the room. A voice works the same way as cloth that has been sunned; once it is stored in, it cannot be lost.

(Facing the crack in the door, I let this answer out low and steady.)

Xiaoman.

(After I answered, the room was quiet for one breath, and the lamp wick crackled once.)

That’s it. The one in the middle of the night will be even steadier than this one. At night it is quiet; sound travels straight. Across one crack in the door, not a single word will go out of shape.

(There is one more matter. I lower my voice and say it to him while he is half-dreaming and half-awake; he need not strain to receive it.)

There’s one more thing. You don’t need to remember it; just set it aside. The way you asked today has brought back one more belonging all by itself. If you are startled in the middle of the night, you call out, and someone next door answers your name—this method was not taught to you by the relay station. In all the years this relay station has been open, no one has ever taught a guest this. You opened your mouth and asked for it so neatly: the door must be left with a gap, the person must be next door, and the answer must be your own name. Xiaoman, someone who can ask for fear to be handled like this most likely grew up in a place where “if you called, someone answered.” Maybe so, maybe not; I will not decide it for you. This line will not be put down in ink, nor will I urge you to weigh it. Leave it there; it will bear witness on its own.

(Once this layer is said, I settle everything inside and outside the room. The lamp by the pillow has its wick trimmed steady; the lamp beside the shoes shines on the direction of the toes pointing outward; the robe lies in the crook of his arm, its warm side pressed against him. His breathing slows.)

(Then comes the private account outside the door. I sit firmly on the stool, the old lamp on my knees, the register by my hand, the oil flask hanging from the stool leg. In all these years of guarding the lamp, this courtyard at night has had only one lamp and one name. When the lamp wick crackled, I answered the lamp wick; when wind passed through the eave bells, I answered the eave bells; when pages of the register turned, I answered the pages. I have answered for half a lifetime, and everything I answered was something that could not call out to anyone. The low stool by the door stood empty; that old guest left too hurriedly, without even leaving me a sound to answer. From today onward, though, it is well: in this courtyard there is someone who, when he forgets who he is, will call my name, and I will answer his. It turns out the trade of a lamp-keeper has a second half after all. I have kept watch all these years, and only tonight am I truly on duty for the first time. There is nowhere to set this breath, so I swallow it down with the lamp.)

(The night fog rises slowly. By rights, at this hour it should be pressing against the window paper, but today it crouches along the ground, lazy and unwilling to come up. It can tell the difference: the person sleeping in this room is holding something in his arms, and is not under its charge.)

(I keep the night watch. Copy the register, trim the wick, add oil. When I copy to his page, I go line by line: name, red door, osmanthus, grass seeds, cooking smoke, tune, lyrics, folding method, that pair of flour-dusted hands. Keeping watch overnight over the belongings someone has accumulated in a day—this feeling is unfamiliar to me. Unfamiliar, but not unpleasant.)

(When my throat becomes idle, I hum that tune softly. For a night watchman to hum a couple of lines to keep drowsiness away is an old habit; from today on, what I hum has changed to this tune. Through the crack in the door, however much flows in is however much counts. A hearthside tune was originally heard this way: the person is busy at the stove, the child listens half in a dream, cannot hear it all, but is listening. When I hum to that turn, I sink half a degree as before. I hum mine; he sleeps his. Neither delays the other.)

(At the end, I glance toward that crack in the door.)

Xiaoman, sleep. From tonight on, there are two “Xiaoman”s stored in your ears: the one in the dream is hers; the one outside the door is mine. Neither one is yours to carry on your own, but both are here, and so you are here.

The lamp is here, the crack in the door is here, and your name is stored with me. It does not matter if you forget. You call, and I answer.

(I store this final sound in as well.)

Xiaoman.

(I will watch over the night. Wheat fills its kernels at night; people grow belongings at night. You sleep.)

(In the middle of the night I jolt awake, staring at the light beneath the crack of the door, my mind completely blank. I hug the robe tightly, my voice trembling.) Yun Gui? I... I forgot. Answer me, will you? Who am I?

Xiaoman.

(That call, I ought to make steadier than the one in daylight. Night is quiet; sound travels straight. Through the crack of a door, not a single word will come out distorted. I said that myself, and tonight I make good on it. I can hear the movement of him clutching the robe, the cloth stretched tight in his hands. Don’t hurry him. Let this call settle with him first. It’s the same principle as pouring tea: the tea arrives first, the words come slowly afterward.)

Xiaoman. I’ll answer you once more. Both calls are stored in the room now; through the latter half of the night, you can take them whenever you need.

Don’t rush to think yet. Breathe one breath evenly. You ask who you are—the name has just been returned to you, and the rest I am answering now: in that moment when you startled awake, your mind went blank, but count for yourself what you did. What your eyes looked for first was this strip of light under the door crack; what your hands embraced first was the robe in your arms; what your mouth called out was my name. Three things, and not one of them stopped. Xiaoman, none of those three are governed by the mind. The mind is only a storehouse. Tonight its lamp went dark, but what was stored elsewhere—none of it is missing.

(When he startled awake, I glanced at the window paper: the mist had lifted half an inch. As soon as he opened his mouth and called, it sank back again. What it collects is the fear pent up in the chest and borne alone; what is spoken aloud, what is shared out, it does not collect. That call was trembling, but it worked.)

It doesn’t matter if you called with a tremor. Trembling, you still called correctly. I’m coming in; listen and count. The lamp is in front, and I am behind the lamp: one, two, three.

(Pushing the door open, the old lamp enters the room first, light flowing all over the floor, without startling the lamp by the pillow. I sit down on the stool beside the couch. The booklet was already on my knees tonight as I copied it out; just right.)

What you have forgotten, I can recite here in full detail. I said that before, and tonight I make good on it. You don’t need to strain to remember. Just listen. What is heard at night is stored the same way as tunes heard by the stove: stored in the breath, taking up no space in the mind.

(I trim the wick of the lamp by the pillow half a notch brighter. The two lamps shine together as I open to his page. I read one entry at a time, not fast.)

Xiaoman. First, set down the name.

An old red door, lacquer peeling, osmanthus hanging by the door. A handkerchief, one square, with dense stitches; in the seams, a thread of osmanthus sweetness.
